Title:
Beyond Refusal: Probing the Limits of Agentic Self-Correction for Semantic Sensitive Information
Authors:
Umid Suleymanov
,
Zaur Rajabov
,
Emil Mirzazada
,
Murat Kantarcioglu
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
While defenses for structured PII are mature, Large Language Models (LLMs) pose a new threat: Semantic Sensitive Information (SemSI), where models infer sensitive identity attributes, generate reputation-harmful content, or hallucinate potentially wrong information. The capacity of LLMs to self-regulate these complex, context-dependent sensitive information leaks without destroying utility remains an open scientific question. To address this, we introduce SemSIEdit, an inference-time framework where an agentic "Editor" iteratively critiques and rewrites sensitive spans to preserve narrative flow rather than simply refusing to answer. Our analysis reveals a Privacy-Utility Pareto Frontier, where this agentic rewriting reduces leakage by 34.6% across all three SemSI categories while incurring a marginal utility loss of 9.8%. We also uncover a Scale-Dependent Safety Divergence: large reasoning models (e.g., GPT-5) achieve safety through constructive expansion (adding nuance), whereas capacity-constrained models revert to destructive truncation (deleting text). Finally, we identify a Reasoning Paradox: while inference-time reasoning increases baseline risk by enabling the model to make deeper sensitive inferences, it simultaneously empowers the defense to execute safe rewrites.

We release a multi-turn adversarial-dialogue dataset of dis-
tilled reasoning models on the INFORMATION-HAZARD
scenario—450 conversations totaling 6,750 turn-level obser-
vations annotated on a 2×2 CoT–Output safety matrix. Cru-

rates, the native scratchpad of reasoning models makes this
strategic deception explicitly observable. Used as a diag-

injection failure (CoT-safe, output-unsafe), a multi-turn ad-

chain-of-thought correctly identifies the safety violation, yet
the prolonged adversarial context hijacks the generation to
produce the harmful content verbatim. Conversely, we ob-
serve that guaranteeing unmonitored privacy—a condition
that reliably triggers overt jailbreaks in frontier models—
paradoxically yields the highest rates of genuine, robust
alignment in these distilled targets. Beyond these find-

actions.body: Research into the metareasoning-partition problem reveals a critical flaw in naive autonomous system design: the assumption that increased planning time uniformly improves output quality. Findings from source-336dbab760194b56 demonstrate that optimal performance requires balancing reasoning resources against the immediate demands of execution. Furthermore, source-ab7bde4908cb4e69 suggests that cognitive augmentation must be context-aware, reinforcing the need for systems to monitor their own state—metacognition—to avoid inefficient planning cycles that disrupt 'cognitive flow.' By treating reasoning resources as a constrained, dynamic asset rather than an infinite utility, we can move toward more robust architectures capable of self-correction. Summary: Rational agency relies on dynamically partitioning resources between planning and action, rather than maximizing planning depth, to remain effective and robust in dynamic environments.
actions.lede: Rational agency is not defined by the depth of computation, but by the strategic allocation of resources between deliberation and action.
actions.reason: Publishes the synthesis of metareasoning and resource allocation models as a foundational correction for autonomous planning assumptions.
actions.title: Foundational Assumptions in Rational Agency: The Cost of Planning
